note: Standing judgments for scripts/apply_vocabulary.py's REVIEW list: occurrences of a
retired or imprecise word that have been read in place and found correct. Every entry
carries the reason, because the point of the list is that the next round reads reasons
Two scopes. A 'line' judgment clears one occurrence and is anchored on verbatim text
from its own line, so it stops applying if that sentence is rewritten. A 'file'
judgment clears a word throughout one document and must say, in 'requires', what makes
that legitimate -- normally the definition the document gives the word. If the
definition goes, the allowance goes with it and every occurrence returns.
A judgment that matches nothing is reported as STALE and fails --check. An allowance
for prose that has moved is a claim nobody checked.

judgments.requires: the audit registry (Section~S25) uses \emph{guard} for a tool's
judgments.reason: The supplement defines the word in its 'On the vocabulary' block, as the audit registry's term for a tool's own conditional of the admission-condition kind, 'where the word names a code path rather than the benchmark's'. That is exactly what the co-author's pass asked for -- define once, then use -- and the fifteen uses are all the registry sense. The paper, which gives no such definition, uses 'admission condition' throughout and contains no 'guard' at all.

This is the sentence that defines the term: it introduces 'timestamp resolution' and gives 'quantum' as its name in the same breath. Retiring the word here would remove the definition rather than the jargon.

judgments.anchor: the millisecond quantum of Section~\mainModeB{} came from the benchmark
judgments.reason: Use after definition, and the sentence is about where the millisecond quantum came from -- the benchmark's own timestamp, not a choice of ours. 'The millisecond timestamp resolution of Section VI came from the benchmark' says the same thing more heavily in a sentence answering an objection, where brevity is the argument.

judgments.anchor: and the instrument is not among them
judgments.reason: The sentence closes a survey of twenty-seven benchmark efforts by naming what the survey judged overlooked. The measuring instrument as a category is precisely the subject -- no substitution of 'timestamp resolution' or 'the benchmark tool' preserves it, because the point is that the survey names no part of the instrument at all.

Use after the definition three sections earlier, and the substitution does not survive it: samples pile up ON a discrete value, and 'pile up on the timestamp resolution' names a property rather than the grid the values land on. The sentence is about what an operator SEES in Pulsar's output, which is a spike at one millisecond.

judgments.anchor: on a sub-quantum path is most of them
judgments.reason: A compound adjective in a table caption, where the alternative is 'a path shorter than the timestamp resolution' and the caption is already six lines. The supplement's vocabulary block says it uses the paper's terms, and the paper defines the quantum as the timestamp resolution.

The other sense of the word: two research groups reaching the same rule by separate routes, which is a fact about provenance and says nothing about whether any two delays are correlated. It is flagged only because the neighbouring clause names timestamps, and the pattern reaches back across a clause on purpose. Cleared as written.

judgments.anchor: with one cause are not independent
judgments.reason: This is the claim itself, and it is negated: the reporting rule that says two delays sharing a scheduler are not independent, carrying the measured correlation and the mispricing factor in the next line. The entry exists to protect this sentence, not to question it.

The same claim applied to the clocksource threat, and negated again: the spread we see is one shared scheduling delay rather than two granularities landing separately. Saying it the other way round would contradict the measurement, which is what this entry watches for.
The supplement's statement of the same negated claim, distinguishing a shared scheduling delay from per-event quantization. The contrast is the point of the sentence and the word carries it.
